name: After Hours Agenda
summary: A brand-led streetwear storefront that keeps product, payment, and made-to-order fulfillment connected.
challenge: The brand needed a storefront that did not flatten its point of view into a generic template.
Product drops needed a practical path without a pile of disconnected tools.
approach: Built a custom storefront around the brand and product details.
Connected Square payments to APLIIQ made-to-order printing and shipping.
delivered: A live storefront for Little Fight’s own streetwear label.
One product, payment, and fulfillment path for a new drop.
outcome: A new product drop can go out in a day.
This is Little Fight’s own product, not a third-party client result.
imageAlt: After Hours Agenda storefront artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: After Hours Agenda is Little Fight’s own streetwear experiment. The project replaces a template-led storefront with one that holds the brand, product details, payment, and shipping together.
Square handles payment and APLIIQ handles made-to-order printing and shipping. Each handoff is clear enough to publish a new drop without rebuilding the store.

name: All Pets Animal Hospital
summary: A public project record that intentionally withholds private client details until public proof is approved.
challenge: The work is real, but public client proof and details are not ready to share.
approach: Kept the work private rather than using a temporary link or invented launch story.
delivered: A proof-pending project record.
outcome: No client result, launch, location, or project image is claimed.
imageAlt: Little Fight Examples artwork. This proof-pending case has no public project image.
narrative: The work is real, but the client details and public proof are not ready to share. The customer path, project date, and changes stay private until the owner approves public proof.
No temporary link is presented as a finished client launch.

name: Army & Navy Bags
type: Private client concept — not a public launch
summary: A phone-first neighborhood field guide for a distinctive local shop.
challenge: The old website acted mostly like a listing and did not explain why a new neighbor or traveler should visit.
The concept needed to retain the shop’s real Lower East Side character without turning it into a generic retail template.
approach: Built a phone-first path from store character to product groups, hours, call, and directions.
Used a neighborhood map to situate the shop near familiar nearby stops.
delivered: A private concept with real-shop imagery, product groups, local facts, and one-tap directions.
Desktop, tablet, and phone concept proof.
outcome: A private client concept, not a public client launch.
imageAlt: Army & Navy Bags concept artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: The concept treats the store as part of a Lower East Side walk. It begins by showing the place and what it carries, then keeps practical visit details close.
It is a private concept designed to show an approach. It is not a public client launch.

name: Brothers Pizzeria
type: Private client concept — not a public storefront
summary: A neighborhood-pizzeria concept that puts heritage, a full readable menu, and phone ordering together.
challenge: The initial digital menu buried the family story and compressed the price grid on smaller screens.
The design needed to bring the shop’s history forward while preserving all menu details and prices.
approach: Reframed the page as a printed neighborhood handbill with the family story before ordering.
Designed menu lines to stack cleanly on phones and kept the call action close.
delivered: A private concept with a complete menu, every published price, phone-first ordering, and a matching brand kit.
Desktop, tablet, and phone concept proof.
outcome: A private client concept with no public-launch or business-performance claim.
imageAlt: Brothers Pizzeria concept artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: The concept centers the family history and keeps it connected to practical menu and ordering tasks. It is built as a readable neighborhood handbill rather than a generic restaurant page.
It remains a private concept, not a live public storefront.

name: CC Films
summary: An official film home that gives fans, press, and premiere guests direct paths to what each needs.
challenge: Marrow needed one official online home without losing the film’s mood.
Fans, press, and premiere guests each needed different material.
approach: Built responsive film pages around the client’s poster, material, and credits.
Gave the trailer, press sources, credits, contact choices, and premiere archive distinct routes.
delivered: Film website and responsive layouts.
Premiere photo archive with event context and photographer credit.
Connected press and contact paths.
outcome: Live at ccfilms.net with separate routes for viewers, press, and premiere guests.
imageAlt: CC Films website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: CC Films needed atmosphere and clear facts at the same time. The site makes the trailer, press sources, credits, and archive legible without asking each audience to navigate through another audience’s task.
The client supplied the film material. Film credits and premiere photography remain with their original creators; Little Fight built the website, gallery, and connected paths.

name: Chromatic Painting & Design
summary: One studio identity with distinct paths for painting projects and mural commissions.
challenge: Painting and mural work share craft but begin with different customer questions.
The site had to show both without splitting the studio into two brands.
approach: Built work pages and layouts around client project images.
Separated painting and mural routes and placed relevant inquiry choices beside each.
delivered: Website and project portfolio.
Distinct painting and mural service paths.
Project-specific inquiry links.
outcome: Live at chromaticaz.com with distinct customer paths for painting and murals.
imageAlt: Chromatic Painting & Design website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The design puts project work ahead of a generic service list. Painting and mural pages retain one studio identity while giving visitors the right question and inquiry route for the job they have.
The studio supplies its work and business facts; Little Fight gives that information a clear home.

name: ClearHelp
summary: A resource-finding site that starts with people’s situations and locations, with a separate route for offering help.
challenge: People seeking food, housing, or other resources may have little time, energy, or privacy.
Finding help and offering help needed distinct starting points.
approach: Organized public paths around needs, ZIP search, plain-language navigation, and resource information.
Kept quick-exit guidance visible and separated public use from private staff work.
delivered: Public website and need-based paths.
ZIP search, resource information, and nearby guidance.
Separate public paths for people seeking and offering help.
outcome: Live at clearhelp.org with separate first steps for finding help and offering it.
imageAlt: ClearHelp website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: ClearHelp begins with a situation or place, instead of assuming someone knows an agency name. Familiar language and category paths lead into the resource directory.
Quick Exit stays visible, along with its limit: leaving the page does not erase browser history.

name: Easy Tiger Bar
summary: A neighborhood-bar site with a readable menu, event paths, visit details, and a separate editing flow for upkeep.
challenge: Guests needed current menu, events, and directions.
The bar also needed a practical way to prepare updates without exposing drafts to guests.
approach: Built menu, events, gallery, and visit pages around supplied bar photography.
Created a focused menu-and-event-poster editing flow and one maintained QR menu destination.
delivered: Guest website, readable text menu, gallery, events, and visit paths.
Menu QR page and a separate draft-to-publication editing flow.
outcome: Live at easytigerglendale.com with one maintained menu address and a draft-to-publication editing flow.
imageAlt: Easy Tiger Bar website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The guest-facing experience lets people see the room, read the menu as text, check events, and choose a map route. The same maintained menu page supports navigation and QR use.
On the owner side, the flow separates saved menu drafts from publication so a change can be prepared before guests see it.

name: Grand Funding LLC
summary: A real-estate funding site that separates project education and planning examples from a transaction-specific review.
challenge: Home purchase, repair, and new-build projects each raise different questions.
The site needed useful planning paths without implying an automatic loan decision.
approach: Created separate project and loan-topic pages.
Connected planning inputs, an explained example, and a deal-review contact route.
delivered: Responsive website and project-type paths.
Funding-information pages and a planning panel.
Contact choices for transaction-specific review.
outcome: Live at grandfundingllc.com. Planning figures are examples, not offers or approvals.
imageAlt: Grand Funding LLC website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: Each project type gets a clear starting route, then gives a visitor room to understand the relevant topic and prepare basic facts for a conversation.
The planning panel can explain inputs, but Grand Funding reviews the deal and sets loan terms.

name: Hair By Rachel Charles
summary: A salon site that helps a visitor understand services before booking, while keeping Square in the booking path.
challenge: A new client needs to know what to choose, what it may cost, and how to book.
Not every visitor is ready to select a service immediately.
approach: Built service paths and phone views around Rachel’s work and portrait.
Connected prices, first-visit guidance, and the Hair Brief before the Square booking handoff.
delivered: Website design, service pages, and Hair Brief experience.
Public booking path that retains Square.
outcome: Live at hairbyrachelcharles.com with service guidance, the Hair Brief, and a Square booking path.
imageAlt: Hair By Rachel Charles website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The site makes room for two kinds of visitor: someone ready to book and someone who only knows their hair goal. The Hair Brief offers the second visitor a separate place to start.
Square was retained instead of replaced. Service details, pricing, and first-visit context precede the booking calendar.

name: Legacy Music Group
type: Client work — reviewed release candidate, not a public client launch
summary: A music-company release candidate with paths for artists, services, booking, company context, and reference material.
challenge: The label needed an official source for artists, services, booking, company context, and search systems without losing its independent character.
approach: Built a control-room visual system with readable paths for essential information.
Reviewed the release candidate across desktop, tablet, and phone.
delivered: A reviewed release candidate with 22 routes for artists, services, booking, and company context.
Responsive proof across three screen sizes.
outcome: Final approved photography, the production booking connection, and the client-owned domain remain release gates.
imageAlt: Legacy Music Group release-candidate artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: The experience uses atmosphere to frame the label, then keeps artists, services, booking, and company information readable. It is a reviewed release candidate.
It does not route visitors to a temporary hosting address. Final photography, the production booking connection, and the client-owned domain still need to be in place before launch.

name: Logan Loans
summary: A mortgage-information site that gives buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors distinct routes to learn before contacting the lender.
challenge: Different audiences arrive with different questions, which a single generic sales page cannot explain well.
approach: Built responsive layouts and routes for buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors.
Connected public guides, planning tools, and contact paths while keeping planning separate from loan offers.
delivered: Website design, audience paths, public guides, planning tools, and contact options.
outcome: Live at logan.loans. Planning figures help people prepare questions; loan terms remain with the lender.
imageAlt: Logan Loans website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The site sorts a broad mortgage topic by visitor situation. Readers can browse guides and planning tools before choosing a contact path.
A calculator result is not a loan offer; the lender confirms terms after reviewing the person, property, and loan.

challenge: The project is real but has no approved public proof or client detail available to share.

delivered: A proof-pending project record.
outcome: No public project outcome is claimed.

narrative: Client details and launch proof stay private until the owner approves their release.
This project is proof pending and is not a specific live-result claim.

name: Public House Creative
type: Client work — private software in production
summary: Cockpit is a private estimating system that brings documents, room classification, price drivers, and reporting into one checkable workspace.
challenge: Estimating was spread across documents, spreadsheets, emails, and a senior estimator’s knowledge.
The team needed one internal system without replacing the estimator’s judgment.
approach: Built Cockpit as a private web app for structured intake, classification, price-driver resolution, and report export.
Designed dense screens to keep source context and confidence visible.
delivered: A private estimating application for real estimates.
Structured room and driver workflow plus report exports.
outcome: Cockpit is in production and used on real estimates. Every number can be traced to its source.
imageAlt: Public House Creative Cockpit process artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: Cockpit takes the messy first pass of an estimate and gives it a structured, reviewable home. Documents, notes, and scope material become rooms, price drivers, and an exportable report.
The estimator remains the final decision-maker. The system makes that judgment more checkable and easier to carry beyond one person.

delivered: A proof-pending project record.
outcome: No public project outcome is claimed.
imageAlt: Little Fight Examples artwork. This proof-pending case has no public project image.

This project is proof pending and is not a finished client proof tile.

name: The Break Room
summary: A pool-hall site that pairs venue character with readable games, menu, directions, and contact details.
challenge: Visitors need the feeling of the venue alongside practical choices about games, food, and a visit.
The site needed to distinguish campaign artwork from photographs of the actual room.
approach: Built a responsive venue site with named activity sections, text menu content, and map/contact paths.
Kept real room photography distinct and labelled separately from campaign artwork.
delivered: Venue website, game and menu sections, and paths to visit information.
outcome: Live at thebreakroompoolhall.com with games, menu, directions, and contact paths in one public home.
imageAlt: The Break Room website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The site helps a visitor explore the room, activities, menu, and visit details from one public home. Its opening visual sets a campaign tone, while labeled room photography supplies factual venue context.
When event or visit information needs current confirmation, the site gives a direct contact route rather than making up an answer.

name: The Tarot Hotline
summary: A personal-service site that explains voice notes, live talks, and a question-first path before a visitor chooses a paid next step.
challenge: Visitors may know their question but not which reading format fits.
The site needed to explain each format before its related form, time choice, or Square payment step.
approach: Built a visual system around the hotline identity and clear service cards.
Created service-choice pages, first-reading guidance, and a separate Ask Rachel option.
delivered: Website, reading-format pages, first-reading guidance, and connected inquiry and payment paths.
outcome: Live at thetarothotline.com with clear reading-format choices, question-first guidance, and connected payment paths.
imageAlt: The Tarot Hotline website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: A visitor sees the difference between a voice note and a live talk before choosing a next step. The free Ask Rachel option gives an unsure person a way to begin without treating a paid reading as the only route.
Service format, scope, price, and next step stay clear before checkout.

name: VenueCircuit
type: Little Fight product — public open beta
summary: A financial operating system for independent venues that keeps bar, door, staff, and promoter splits in one traceable closeout flow.
challenge: Independent venues often close nights across spreadsheets and separate systems, blurring venue and promoter money.
approach: Built the full public product around a nightly close, split tracking, drill-down reports, and the way venue teams run a night.
delivered: Venue financial software with nightly close, split tracking, and receipt-level drill-down.
outcome: Live in open beta at venuecircuit.app with a nightly close of about 90 seconds. This is Little Fight’s own product.
imageAlt: VenueCircuit product artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: VenueCircuit brings the pieces of a venue night—bar, door, staff, and promoter splits—into one product while keeping the venue’s money and promoter money distinct.
It is Little Fight’s own public open-beta product, built from first sketch into software that venues can use.

name: DeckSpace
summary: An onboard guide, guest network, and memory layer built around the little world of a cruise.
challenge: Guests need events, venue hours, and each other without digging through a dashboard.
approach: Keep the nostalgic heart of cruising and organize discovery around the voyage.
delivered: An archived product walkthrough covering onboard discovery, profiles, events, and shared photos.
outcome: Retained captures show the intended discovery path. The former host is not presented as a current launch.
